name: Battle of Chacabuco
info: The Army of the Andes under José de San Martín defeated a royalist force under Rafael Maroto at Chacabuco, north of Santiago, on 12 February 1817, and entered the Chilean capital within days, where O'Higgins became Supreme Director.

facts.date: 12 February 1817; one account puts the end of the fighting at 14:00
facts.place: The Hacienda de Chacabuco in the valley of Chacabuco, Colina, about 55 km north of Santiago, Chile
facts.sides: The Army of the Andes, of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and Chilean exiles, under Captain General José de San Martín with Miguel Estanislao Soler and Bernardo O'Higgins, in two columns of 2,000 and 1,500 men by one account; a royalist force under Brigadier Rafael Maroto of about 1,500 men, with up to 2,000 in another account
facts.outcome: The patriot army won. Royalist dead are given as 500 and prisoners as 600; patriot dead as 12. The patriots entered Santiago within days and O'Higgins was named Supreme Director of Chile.

t: San Martín split his army into two columns to take the royalists from front and rear, but O'Higgins's column attacked before Soler's arrived, and accounts of what followed differ.
The royalists were fewer, about 1,500 men, and their governor had reversed the decision to retreat south the morning after it was taken, ordering Maroto to hold Chacabuco.
San Martín declined the post of governor of Chile and an assembly of notable residents named O'Higgins Supreme Director, opening the period known as the Patria Nueva.
dyk: Black soldiers, mostly freed former slaves recruited in the interior provinces, are estimated at between 2,000 and 3,000 of the Army of the Andes, and made up the majority of its 7th, 8th and 11th Infantry Regiments.
ev: The defeat at Rancagua ends the Patria Vieja, and Chilean exiles place themselves under San Martín in Cuyo
The Army of the Andes sets out from Mendoza to cross the Andes, losing as much as one third of its men and more than half of its horses
The royalist conference at Santiago adopts Maroto's plan to retreat south on 8 February, and the governor reverses it the next morning
The patriot columns meet at the camp of Curimón on 9 February and resolve to attack at dawn on the 12th
The two patriot divisions come down on the royalists at Chacabuco on 12 February, and the fighting ends in the afternoon
The patriots enter Santiago, on 13 February by one account and 14 February by another
San Martín declines the governorship and an assembly names O'Higgins Supreme Director
The expulsion of Spanish forces from Chile is completed at the Battle of Maipú

sections.background:
After the defeat at Rancagua in 1814, which ended the period of Chilean history called the Patria Vieja, Chilean exiles went to Cuyo and placed themselves under José de San Martín, governor of the province. San Martín planned to defeat the royalists by attacking the Viceroyalty of Peru by sea from Chile, and the royalist occupation of Chile obliged him to free that country first. Bernardo O'Higgins and Ramón Freire helped to organise and train the Army of the Andes. San Martín freed black slaves on condition that they enlisted, and took into the army the Chilean soldiers who followed O'Higgins and those of Carrera willing to serve under his flags.

In January 1817 the army set out across the Andes. San Martín's planning misled the royalist forces in Chile into defending against threats that did not exist, and the crossing went unchallenged. It was costly all the same: the army lost as much as one third of its men and more than half of its horses. The columns that crossed by the Los Patos road and by the Uspallata road met at the camp of Curimón on 9 February.

The royalists found it hard to gather an army because their forces were scattered. At a military conference on 8 February, called by the Royal Governor, Field Marshal Casimiro Marcó del Pont, the plan of Brigadier Rafael Maroto was adopted: to give up Santiago and retreat south, where the royalists could regroup and gather resources. The following morning the governor reversed the decision and ordered Maroto to prepare for battle at Chacabuco.
sections.forces:
Estimates of the size of the Army of the Andes run from as low as 3,500 to as high as 6,000 men. One account of the build-up speaks of approximately 6,000 men, 1,200 horses and 22 cannons; another of about 4,000 Chileans and Argentines, well armed and disciplined. About 1,200 auxiliaries handled supply. Black soldiers, mostly freed slaves, are estimated at between 2,000 and 3,000, and Lynch puts the freedmen recruited at 1,554.

For the battle San Martín divided his troops in two, to attack the royalists from front and rear. The right wing, under Miguel Estanislao Soler, was to attack from the west with the 1st Cazadores and 11th battalions, companies of the 7th and 8th, a squadron of Grenadiers, the commander-in-chief's escort squadron and seven guns: 2,000 men in all. The left wing, under O'Higgins, was to attack from the east with fusilier companies of the 7th and 8th, three squadrons of Horse Grenadiers and two guns: 1,500 men. Soler took the Montenegro road, gentler but much longer; O'Higgins took the Cuesta Vieja, shorter but steep and far more dangerous. Another account has San Martín divide 2,000 troops in all.

The royalists were fewer: the Talavera battalion of peninsular soldiers and two others drawn mainly from Chiloé and Valdivia, about 1,500 men, though another account has Maroto leading up to 2,000 volunteers. Their morale was low, as they were badly paid and had not had their ranks from the earlier reconquest recognised. A spy disguised as a roto, a poor Chilean peasant, kept San Martín informed of Marcó's orders and Maroto's plans.
sections.course:
San Martín sent his troops down the mountain from midnight on 11 February to attack at dawn. Soler's column took longer than expected. O'Higgins met the royalist advance parties and then their main body, and deployed on the hill Los Halcones, sending word to San Martín. Maroto, finding the slope held by the patriots on the 12th, chose to defend the ground near the hacienda rather than fall back to Colina.

Accounts of the next hours differ. In one, O'Higgins, receiving no orders, began the attack; San Martín sent word to Soler and went forward himself with O'Higgins until a division of Soler's advance arrived and enveloped the royalists' left flank and rear. In another, O'Higgins, supposedly overcome by the sight of his homeland, abandoned the plan and charged with 1,500 men; he claimed the royalists had stopped retreating and were advancing, and that retreating up the narrow path would have meant being picked off one by one. San Martín ordered Soler to charge the flank.

A third version says O'Higgins's charge was repulsed with many casualties. At 11:45, against orders not to commit fire and on the advice of the former Napoleonic officer Crámer, he sent two bayonet columns against the Talavera battalion on the royalist right, with Zapiola's cavalry. The grenadiers were stopped by the channel of Las Margaritas and fell back to Los Halcones before charging again. Zapiola broke the square of the Talaveras and the royalists fled towards the houses of Chacabuco, leaving a third of their strength. In the other accounts the royalists form a square round the ranch and the fighting is hand to hand there.
sections.aftermath:
Royalist dead are given as 500 and prisoners as 600, one account specifying 32 officers and 600 soldiers. The Army of the Andes lost twelve men in the battle; one account adds 120 who died of wounds, another counts 120 wounded. The captured goods included the flag of the Chiloé regiment, about a thousand rifles and two guns. Maroto escaped, slightly wounded, thanks to the speed of his horse.

The patriots entered Santiago, on 13 February by one account and 14 February by another. Several historians think San Martín erred in not pursuing the beaten royalists, who were able to re-embark 1,600 soldiers for Peru, the base of Mariano Osorio's expedition; otherwise, they estimate, the expedition to Peru would not have been delayed three years. Another account has the remaining royalists retreat to the south of Chile, form a small enclave, be reinforced by sea and in the end withdraw by sea to Lima.

An assembly under the interim governor Francisco Ruiz-Tagle first named San Martín governor of Chile. He refused and called a new assembly of 210 notable residents, and the army's auditor Bernardo de Vera y Pintado repeated his refusal; O'Higgins was acclaimed Supreme Director and held the post until 1823. His first act of government, on 17 February, was a proclamation. News of the victory reached Mendoza on 16 February and Buenos Aires on 24 February.
sections.sources:
San Martín sent an official report to Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, Supreme Director of the United Provinces, soon after the battle, and the figures for the dead and the prisoners are given in that connection. The fighting itself is told in more than one way. O'Higgins gave his own reasons for leaving the plan, and what took place between his advance and Soler's arrival is fiercely debated. One version has Soler's advance division arrive and complete the envelopment; another has O'Higgins's charge repulsed, with Soler hurrying to save the day, and credits the advice of the Napoleonic officer Crámer.

The figures are disputed as well. Estimates of the Army of the Andes run from 3,500 to 6,000 men, the crossing is dated from 17 or 19 January and given 21 or 25 days, and the entry into Santiago falls on 13 or 14 February. It is not agreed whether 120 patriots were wounded or died of their wounds, nor how many royalists got away: Maroto escaped, and 1,600 soldiers are said to have embarked for Peru.
sections.legacy:
The victory began the expulsion of Spanish forces from Chile, completed the following year at the Battle of Maipú. It ended the period of the Reconquista, or Restoration, and began the Patria Nueva, with O'Higgins in office until 1823. The Chilean army was reconstituted under Argentine officers, and San Martín was appointed commander of the United Army, which joined the Army of the Andes with Chilean troops and fought Osorio's royalist army at Cancha Rayada and Maipú.

The battle raised the morale of the Army of the Andes and is placed within the wider movement of liberation from Spanish rule across South America, in which San Martín was one of the leaders. He refused the governorship in accordance with his own resolve and instructions from Buenos Aires, and the Chilean state that followed was led by O'Higgins, who had fought in the left wing at Chacabuco.

Several ships of the Chilean Navy have been named after the battle, and a Monument to the Victory of Chacabuco commemorates it. The flag taken from the Chiloé regiment was carried to Buenos Aires with San Martín's report by Major Manuel Escalada on 26 February.

summary: At Chacabuco on 12 February 1817 the Army of the Andes under San Martín defeated a royalist force of about 1,500 under Maroto, and entered Santiago within days. Accounts of the fighting differ; O'Higgins became Supreme Director of Chile.
notes: Strengths conflict: English battle article says San Martín divided 2,000 troops and O'Higgins charged with 1,500; Spanish gives Soler 2,000 and O'Higgins 1,500. Army size 3,500-6,000 (Army of the Andes article), about 6,000 (battle article), about 4,000 (Spanish).

Dates conflict: crossing begins 17 January (battle article) or 19 January (Crossing article), 21 or 25 days; war council 11 February 'three days before intended attack' (English) against attack on 12th (Spanish): I left that sentence out; Santiago entered 13 February (Crossing article) or 14 February (Spanish).
Patriot losses: English says 12 killed and 120 died of wounds; Spanish says 12 dead and 120 wounded.

English says every royalist was killed or captured at the ranch, which contradicts Maroto's escape and the 1,600 who re-embarked (Spanish): I omitted 'every'. The English also says the royalists' reinforcements came from Santiago and the Spanish from the south: left out.
Garbled in the Spanish article: 'San Martín llama a Osorio, el general realista, para que saque a sus heridos': Osorio was not in command; left out. The Spanish battle order lists are empty.

Left out: Quintanilla's advice to retreat and Maroto's general order, a judgement on Maroto's pride; the Spanish article's text of San Martín's report and Pueyrredón's message; judgemental phrases (heroically, mini Spanish Chile).
